Section 1.1 — What Ethics Is, Why It Is Necessary, and What It Is For

Every man who stands to preach is already an ethicist, whether he has ever used the word or not. The moment he tells a congregation what they ought to do, he has made a claim about right and wrong, and behind that claim stands some authority. The only question is which one. So before we ever ask what is the right thing to do, we have to ask a deeper question: who has the right to tell me what right is? That question is where Christian ethics begins, and it is where it parts ways with almost everything the world will offer you.

Let me give you the plain definition first and then unfold it. Christian ethics is the disciplined study of how God's people are to live, judged by the standard of God's own character as He has revealed it in His Word. Notice what that definition does. It does not start with us. It does not start with what feels right, what works, or what the majority has decided. It starts with God — with who He is — and it measures every action against Him. Ethics, for the believer, is not the search for a standard. The standard has already been given. Ethics is the careful, prayerful work of learning to live inside it.

Why is such a study necessary? You might think that a man who loves God and reads his Bible would simply know how to act, and to a degree that is true. But Scripture itself assumes otherwise. Paul prays that the Philippians' love would "abound still more and more in knowledge and all discernment, that you may approve the things that are excellent" (Philippians 1:9–10). Discernment is not automatic. It is trained. The writer of Hebrews rebukes believers who ought to be teachers but still need milk, because "solid food belongs to those who are of full age, that is, those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil" (Hebrews 5:14). Hear that phrase — by reason of use. Ethical maturity is not a gift dropped on the new convert. It is the fruit of exercise, of practice, of a mind drilled again and again in the things of God until it can tell good from evil the way a trained ear tells a true note from a flat one.

And what is it all for? Here the world and the church diverge completely. The world studies ethics to make society function, to keep people from destroying one another, to be happy. None of those are bad things. But they are not the goal. The goal of Christian ethics is the glory of God. "Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31). That single verse reorders the entire enterprise. We do not pursue holiness to feel good about ourselves, or even mainly to help others, though it will do both. We pursue it because a holy God is worthy of a holy people, and because every right thing we do puts His character on display before a watching world. Ethics is worship with our hands and feet.
Section 1.2 — The Absolute Authority of Scripture

Everything I have just said hangs on one conviction, and if that conviction goes, the whole structure comes down. The conviction is this: that Scripture is the very Word of God, and therefore carries God's own authority over how we live.

"All Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work."<cite>2 Timothy 3:16–17 (NKJV)</cite>

Read that passage slowly, because Paul packs an entire doctrine of ethics into two verses. Scripture is God-breathed — it comes out of the mouth of God as surely as breath comes out of yours. That is its authority. And then notice the four uses Paul gives it: doctrine teaches us what is true, reproof shows us where we have gone wrong, correction sets us back on the path, and instruction in righteousness trains us to walk that path going forward. Teaching, rebuking, correcting, training — that is the full motion of a life being shaped by the Word. And mark the result Paul aims at: that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work. The Word is not merely sufficient to save us. It is sufficient to form us. There is no good work for which Scripture leaves the man of God unequipped.

Cross-Reference · Systematic TheologyThe doctrines of inspiration, inerrancy, and the sufficiency of Scripture are developed at length in the Systematic Theology course (Unit 1, The Doctrine of Revelation).

This is what we mean by the sufficiency of Scripture, and for the pastor it is not an abstraction. It means that when a couple sits across from you with a marriage in pieces, when a young man confesses an addiction he cannot break, when an elder asks how the church should handle a member in open sin — you are not thrown back on your own cleverness or the latest book of techniques. You have a Word from God that is living and powerful, that judges the thoughts and intents of the heart (Hebrews 4:12), and that is able to make the man of God complete. The world will tell you that the Bible is an old book with nothing to say to modern problems. The man who has actually used it in the trenches of ministry knows better.

Now, I want to be careful here, because the authority of Scripture is often misunderstood as a claim that the Bible gives a direct verse for every situation. It does not. There is no chapter and verse on whether to take a particular job or which medical treatment to pursue for a dying parent. But the sufficiency of Scripture does not mean Scripture answers every question by direct command; it means Scripture gives us everything we need — the truth about God, about ourselves, about right and wrong, and the wisdom of a renewed mind — to discern how to honor God in every situation. The Bible is not a card catalog of answers. It is the authoritative foundation on which all right reasoning is built.
Section 1.3 — The Contrast with Secular and Relativistic Approaches

To see what we have, it helps to see clearly what the world offers in its place. Strip away the labels and the academic vocabulary, and several real traditions recur. Consequentialism, including utilitarianism, locates the standard in outcomes: an act is right if it produces the greatest good for the greatest number. Deontological approaches locate it in reason and duty: right is whatever a rational person would will as a universal rule, regardless of outcome. Virtue ethics locates it in character: right action is what a person of practical wisdom would do, aimed at genuine human flourishing. Natural-law traditions — which this course itself draws on later, in its treatment of ordinary and extraordinary means at the end of life — hold that a real moral order is built into human nature and can be known by reason even without special revelation. Some thinkers in each of these traditions defend real, objective moral truth without grounding it explicitly in God; we should engage them honestly rather than caricature them. And some, though by no means all who reject a Christian foundation, land in relativism, the view that there is no fixed right and wrong, only your truth and my truth.

I am not asking you to dismiss these systems as if they contained nothing true. The man who studies consequences is right that actions have results and that love considers them. The relativist has correctly noticed that human judgments are fallible and culturally shaped. The error is never that these views see nothing; the error is where they finally rest their weight. They rest it on the creature. And a standard built on the creature can be no more stable, no more holy, and no more authoritative than the creature himself — which is to say, not very. The most honest secular thinkers admit this. Cut the moral law loose from God and you are left, in the end, with preference dressed up as principle.

Here is the heart of the matter, and I want you to feel its weight as a pastor and not merely understand it as a student. Relativism cannot be lived. The man who tells you there is no objective right and wrong will, the moment you wrong him, appeal to a justice he claims does not exist. He cannot help it, because he is made in the image of God and the work of the law is written on his heart (Romans 2:15). This is your great point of contact with a lost world. You are not importing a foreign morality into people who have none. You are calling them back to the One whose law they already know in their conscience and have spent their lives suppressing. The relativist is not your opponent so much as your mission field, and the law he cannot escape is the schoolmaster meant to bring him to Christ.

Cross-Reference · Doctrinal PreachingThe principle that every person bears God's image and therefore possesses irreducible worth — foundational to the point above — was developed in the Doctrinal Preaching course (Unit 5, Preaching the Doctrine of Man). It returns in Unit 7 of this course (Sanctity of Life).
Section 1.4 — Why Pastors Must Pursue Ethical Formation

Let me close this first unit by speaking to you directly about why this study matters for you in particular, more than for almost any other man in your congregation. There are at least three reasons, and each one should land on you with some weight.

The first is that you are held to a higher account. "My brethren, let not many of you become teachers, knowing that we shall receive a stricter judgment" (James 3:1). The man who teaches others how to live has taken up a burden the ordinary believer has not. God will not grade you on a curve because the work was hard. The teacher is judged as a teacher. That should sober you every time you open the Book to instruct another soul.

The second is that you lead by example, not merely by instruction. Peter charges the elders to shepherd the flock "being examples to the flock" (1 Peter 5:3). Paul can say to the Corinthians, with no false modesty, "Imitate me, just as I also imitate Christ" (1 Corinthians 11:1). This is the heaviest and most searching part of pastoral ethics, and I have said something like it about preaching for years: it is not finally something you do, it is something you are. You can preach a sermon you have not lived, but you cannot pastor a people you are not. The congregation will absorb your character far more deeply than your words, and where the two contradict each other, your character will win the argument every time. A man may forget your finest sermon by Tuesday; he will never forget the year he watched how you treated your wife, or how you handled the deacon who opposed you, or what you did when no one but God was looking.

The third reason is the simplest and the most often forgotten. You pursue ethical formation because the gospel demands it of you as it demands it of every believer — not as the price of your salvation, which Christ has paid in full, but as its proper fruit. "We are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them" (Ephesians 2:10). You were not saved by your good works, but you were most certainly saved for them. The whole of this course rests on that order and never reverses it: grace first, always first, and then the holy life that grace produces. Keep that order straight and ethics becomes the joyful study of how a forgiven man learns to walk worthy of the One who bought him. Reverse it, and ethics curdles into a law that crushes. We will be careful, all the way through, to keep it straight.

mc.stem: 1. Every preacher is already an “ethicist” because the moment he tells a congregation what they ought to do, his claim rests on:
options: some authority over right and wrong
mc.why: To tell people what they ought to do is to make a claim that rests on some authority over right and wrong; the only question is which one.

es_reference.stem: 1. Todo predicador ya es un «eticista», porque en el momento en que dice a una congregación lo que debe hacer, su afirmación descansa sobre:
options: alguna autoridad sobre el bien y el mal
es_reference.why: Decir a las personas lo que deben hacer es hacer una afirmación que descansa sobre alguna autoridad sobre el bien y el mal; la única pregunta es cuál.

mc.stem: 2. Christian ethics, as defined in the unit, measures every action against:
options: the teaching of the early church fathers
mc.why: Christian ethics does not start with us; it measures every action against God’s own character as revealed in His Word.

es_reference.stem: 2. La ética cristiana, según se define en la unidad, mide cada acción frente a:
options: el propio carácter revelado de Dios
la enseñanza de los primeros padres de la iglesia
es_reference.why: La ética cristiana no comienza con nosotros; mide cada acción frente al propio carácter de Dios tal como Él lo ha revelado en su Palabra.

mc.stem: 3. For the believer, the unit says, ethics is NOT primarily:
options: learning to live inside a given standard
mc.why: The standard has already been given; ethics is not the search for one but the work of learning to live inside it.

es_reference.stem: 3. Para el creyente, dice la unidad, la ética NO es principalmente:
options: aprender a vivir dentro de una norma dada
es_reference.why: La norma ya ha sido dada; la ética no es la búsqueda de una, sino la labor de aprender a vivir dentro de ella.

mc.stem: 4. Paul’s prayer in Philippians 1:9–10 is used to show that discernment is:
mc.why: Paul prays that love would abound in knowledge and discernment—showing discernment is trained, not automatic.

es_reference.stem: 4. La oración de Pablo en Filipenses 1:9–10 se usa para mostrar que el discernimiento es:
es_reference.why: Pablo ora para que el amor abunde en ciencia y discernimiento, mostrando que el discernimiento se entrena, no es automático.

mc.stem: 5. The phrase “by reason of use” (Hebrews 5:14) teaches that ethical maturity comes through:
mc.why: Maturity is the fruit of exercise and practice—senses trained by use to discern good and evil.

es_reference.stem: 5. La frase «por el uso» (Hebreos 5:14) enseña que la madurez ética viene por medio de:
options: el ejercicio y la práctica repetida
es_reference.why: La madurez es el fruto del ejercicio y la práctica: los sentidos ejercitados por el uso para discernir el bien y el mal.

mc.stem: 6. The ultimate goal of Christian ethics, according to the unit, is:
mc.why: The goal is the glory of God; a holy God is worthy of a holy people.

es_reference.stem: 6. La meta última de la ética cristiana, según la unidad, es:
es_reference.why: La meta es la gloria de Dios; un Dios santo es digno de un pueblo santo.

mc.stem: 7. The unit summarizes the believer’s ethical life with the phrase:
options: worship with our hands and feet
mc.why: Because every right act displays God’s character, ethics is “worship with our hands and feet.”

es_reference.stem: 7. La unidad resume la vida ética del creyente con la frase:
options: adoración con nuestras manos y pies
es_reference.why: Porque cada acto recto exhibe el carácter de Dios, la ética es «adoración con nuestras manos y pies».

mc.stem: 8. “All Scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2 Timothy 3:16) is explained with the image that Scripture is:
options: a human record of God’s acts
God-breathed, from the mouth of God
mc.why: Scripture is God-breathed—it comes from the mouth of God as breath comes from yours—and that is its authority.

es_reference.stem: 8. «Toda Escritura es dada por inspiración de Dios» (2 Timoteo 3:16) se explica con la imagen de que la Escritura es:
options: un registro humano de los actos de Dios
inspirada por Dios, salida de la boca de Dios
es_reference.why: La Escritura es inspirada por Dios — sale de la boca de Dios como el aliento sale de la suya — y esa es su autoridad.

mc.stem: 9. The four uses of Scripture in 2 Timothy 3:16 are doctrine, reproof, correction, and:
mc.why: Doctrine teaches, reproof rebukes, correction restores, and instruction in righteousness trains us going forward.

es_reference.stem: 9. Los cuatro usos de la Escritura en 2 Timoteo 3:16 son enseñar, redargüir, corregir e:
es_reference.why: La enseñanza enseña, la reprensión redarguye, la corrección restaura, y la instrucción en justicia nos entrena en adelante.

mc.stem: 10. Paul’s aimed-at result in 2 Timothy 3:17 is that the man of God may be:
options: complete and equipped for every good work
mc.why: The Word is sufficient not only to save but to form—making the man of God complete, equipped for every good work.

es_reference.stem: 10. El resultado al que Pablo apunta en 2 Timoteo 3:17 es que el hombre de Dios sea:
options: perfecto y enteramente preparado para toda buena obra
es_reference.why: La Palabra es suficiente no solo para salvar sino para formar, haciendo al hombre de Dios perfecto, enteramente preparado para toda buena obra.

mc.stem: 11. The “sufficiency” of Scripture, as the unit defines it, means Scripture is sufficient to:
options: both save us and form us
mc.why: Sufficiency means the Word is enough not merely to save us but to form us for every good work.

es_reference.stem: 11. La «suficiencia» de la Escritura, según la define la unidad, significa que la Escritura es suficiente para:
options: reemplazar el papel de los pastores
es_reference.why: La suficiencia significa que la Palabra basta no meramente para salvarnos sino para formarnos para toda buena obra.

mc.stem: 12. Which passage describes the Word as living and powerful, judging the thoughts and intents of the heart?
mc.why: Hebrews 4:12 calls the Word living and powerful, judging the thoughts and intents of the heart.

es_reference.stem: 12. ¿Cuál pasaje describe la Palabra como viva y eficaz, que discierne los pensamientos y las intenciones del corazón?
es_reference.why: Hebreos 4:12 llama a la Palabra viva y eficaz, que discierne los pensamientos y las intenciones del corazón.

mc.stem: 13. Properly understood, sufficiency means Scripture gives us everything we need to:
options: discern how to honor God in every situation
mc.why: Sufficiency does not give a verse for every case; it gives everything needed to discern how to honor God in any situation.

es_reference.stem: 13. Entendida correctamente, la suficiencia significa que la Escritura nos da todo lo que necesitamos para:
options: discernir cómo honrar a Dios en cada situación
es_reference.why: La suficiencia no da un versículo para cada caso; da todo lo necesario para discernir cómo honrar a Dios en cualquier situación.

mc.stem: 14. The unit compares the Bible to which image to clarify what sufficiency does NOT mean?
mc.why: The Bible is not a card catalog of direct answers; it is the authoritative foundation on which right reasoning is built.

es_reference.stem: 14. ¿Con cuál imagen compara la unidad la Biblia para aclarar lo que la suficiencia NO significa?
es_reference.why: La Biblia no es un fichero de respuestas directas; es el fundamento autoritativo sobre el cual se edifica todo recto razonamiento.

mc.stem: 15. Nearly all secular ethical systems share the common feature of locating the standard:
options: inside the creation rather than in the Creator
mc.why: Strip away the labels and secular systems rest the standard inside the creation rather than in the Creator.

es_reference.stem: 15. Casi todos los sistemas éticos seculares comparten el rasgo común de ubicar la norma:
options: dentro de la creación en vez de en el Creador
es_reference.why: Quite las etiquetas y los sistemas seculares descansan la norma dentro de la creación en vez de en el Creador.

mc.stem: 16. The decisive error of secular systems, the unit argues, is not what they see but:
options: where they finally rest their weight
mc.why: The error is never that they see nothing true, but that they rest their weight on the creature rather than the Creator.

es_reference.stem: 16. El error decisivo de los sistemas seculares, argumenta la unidad, no es lo que ven sino:
es_reference.why: El error nunca es que no vean nada verdadero, sino que descansan su peso sobre la criatura en vez del Creador.

mc.stem: 17. The unit argues that relativism ultimately cannot be:
mc.why: Relativism cannot be lived: the one who denies objective right will appeal to justice the moment he is wronged.

es_reference.stem: 17. La unidad sostiene que el relativismo finalmente no se puede:
es_reference.why: El relativismo no se puede vivir: el que niega el bien objetivo apelará a la justicia en el momento en que se le agravie.

mc.stem: 18. Which passage grounds the claim that the work of the law is written on every person’s heart?
mc.why: Romans 2:15 says the work of the law is written on the heart—your point of contact with a lost world.

es_reference.stem: 18. ¿Cuál pasaje fundamenta la afirmación de que la obra de la ley está escrita en el corazón de toda persona?
es_reference.why: Romanos 2:15 dice que la obra de la ley está escrita en el corazón — su punto de contacto con un mundo perdido.

mc.stem: 19. The law the unbeliever cannot escape is described as the “schoolmaster” meant to bring him to:
mc.why: The law he cannot escape is the schoolmaster meant to bring him to Christ—so the relativist is a mission field, not an enemy.

es_reference.stem: 19. La ley que el incrédulo no puede escapar se describe como el «ayo» destinado a llevarlo a:
es_reference.why: La ley que no puede escapar es el ayo destinado a llevarlo a Cristo — así el relativista es un campo misionero, no un enemigo.

mc.stem: 20. Ephesians 2:10 establishes the unit’s governing order, which is:
options: grace and works as the joint price of salvation
law and grace held in equal balance
grace first, then the holy life it produces
mc.why: We are saved for good works, not by them: grace first, always first, and then the holy life grace produces.

es_reference.stem: 20. Efesios 2:10 establece el orden rector de la unidad, que es:
options: las obras primero, luego la gracia
la gracia y las obras como precio conjunto de la salvación
la ley y la gracia en equilibrio igual
la gracia primero, luego la vida santa que produce
es_reference.why: Somos salvos para buenas obras, no por ellas: la gracia primero, siempre primero, y luego la vida santa que la gracia produce.

sa.prompt: 21. Define Christian ethics as the unit defines it, and explain what is distinctive about where it begins.
sa.model: Christian ethics is the disciplined study of how God’s people are to live, judged by the standard of God’s own character as He has revealed it in His Word. What is distinctive is where it begins: not with us, not with what feels right or works or commands a majority, but with God and who He is. The standard has already been given; ethics is therefore not the search for a standard but the prayerful work of learning to live inside the one God has revealed.

es_reference.prompt: 21. Defina la ética cristiana tal como la define la unidad, y explique qué hay de distintivo en dónde comienza.
es_reference.model: La ética cristiana es el estudio disciplinado de cómo ha de vivir el pueblo de Dios, juzgado por la norma del propio carácter de Dios tal como Él lo ha revelado en su Palabra. Lo distintivo es dónde comienza: no con nosotros, no con lo que se siente correcto o funciona o manda una mayoría, sino con Dios y con quién es Él. La norma ya ha sido dada; la ética no es la búsqueda de una norma sino la labor llena de oración de aprender a vivir dentro de la que Dios ha revelado.

sa.prompt: 22. Why is the study of ethics necessary if a man already loves God and reads his Bible?
sa.model: Scripture itself assumes discernment is not automatic. Paul prays that the Philippians’ love would abound in knowledge and discernment, and Hebrews rebukes believers who still need milk because solid food belongs to those whose senses are exercised by use to discern good and evil. Ethical maturity is not a gift dropped on the new convert; it is the fruit of exercise and repeated practice, a mind drilled in the things of God until it can tell good from evil as a trained ear tells a true note from a flat one.

es_reference.prompt: 22. ¿Por qué es necesario el estudio de la ética si un hombre ya ama a Dios y lee su Biblia?
es_reference.model: La Escritura misma supone que el discernimiento no es automático. Pablo ora para que el amor de los filipenses abunde en ciencia y discernimiento, y Hebreos reprende a los creyentes que aún necesitan leche, porque el alimento sólido es para los que por el uso tienen los sentidos ejercitados en discernir el bien y el mal. La madurez ética no es un don dejado caer sobre el nuevo convertido; es el fruto del ejercicio y la práctica repetida, una mente entrenada en las cosas de Dios hasta distinguir el bien del mal como un oído entrenado distingue una nota verdadera de una desafinada.

sa.prompt: 23. What is the goal of Christian ethics, and how does it differ from the world’s purpose for studying ethics?
sa.model: The world studies ethics to make society function, to keep people from destroying one another, and to be happy—none of them bad, but none of them the goal. The goal of Christian ethics is the glory of God: whatever we do, we do all to His glory. We pursue holiness not mainly to feel good or even to help others, though it does both, but because a holy God is worthy of a holy people and every right act puts His character on display before a watching world. Ethics is worship with our hands and feet.

es_reference.prompt: 23. ¿Cuál es la meta de la ética cristiana, y en qué difiere del propósito del mundo para estudiar la ética?
es_reference.model: El mundo estudia la ética para hacer funcionar a la sociedad, para impedir que las personas se destruyan y para ser feliz — nada de ello malo, pero nada de ello la meta. La meta de la ética cristiana es la gloria de Dios: todo lo que hacemos, lo hacemos para su gloria. Buscamos la santidad no principalmente para sentirnos bien ni siquiera para ayudar a otros, aunque hace ambas cosas, sino porque un Dios santo es digno de un pueblo santo y cada acto recto pone su carácter en exhibición ante un mundo que observa. La ética es adoración con nuestras manos y pies.

sa.prompt: 24. Explain the authority and the sufficiency of Scripture for ethics from 2 Timothy 3:16–17.
sa.model: Scripture is God-breathed—it comes from the mouth of God—and that is its authority over how we live. Paul gives it four uses: doctrine teaches what is true, reproof shows where we have gone wrong, correction sets us back on the path, and instruction in righteousness trains us to walk it. The aimed-at result is that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work. So the Word is sufficient not only to save us but to form us; there is no good work for which it leaves the man of God unequipped.

es_reference.prompt: 24. Explique la autoridad y la suficiencia de la Escritura para la ética a partir de 2 Timoteo 3:16–17.
es_reference.model: La Escritura es inspirada por Dios — sale de la boca de Dios — y esa es su autoridad sobre cómo vivimos. Pablo le da cuatro usos: la enseñanza enseña lo que es verdad, la reprensión muestra dónde hemos errado, la corrección nos vuelve al camino y la instrucción en justicia nos entrena para andarlo. El resultado al que apunta es que el hombre de Dios sea perfecto, enteramente preparado para toda buena obra. Así la Palabra es suficiente no solo para salvarnos sino para formarnos; no hay buena obra para la cual deje al hombre de Dios sin equipar.

sa.prompt: 25. What does the sufficiency of Scripture NOT mean, and what does it mean?
sa.model: Sufficiency does not mean the Bible gives a direct chapter-and-verse for every situation; there is no verse on which job to take or which treatment to pursue for a dying parent. It means Scripture gives us everything we need—the truth about God, about ourselves, about right and wrong, and the wisdom of a renewed mind—to discern how to honor God in every situation. The Bible is not a card catalog of answers but the authoritative foundation on which all right reasoning is built.

es_reference.prompt: 25. ¿Qué NO significa la suficiencia de la Escritura, y qué sí significa?
es_reference.model: La suficiencia no significa que la Biblia dé un capítulo y versículo directo para cada situación; no hay versículo sobre qué trabajo aceptar o qué tratamiento procurar para un padre moribundo. Significa que la Escritura nos da todo lo que necesitamos — la verdad acerca de Dios, de nosotros mismos, del bien y del mal, y la sabiduría de una mente renovada — para discernir cómo honrar a Dios en cada situación. La Biblia no es un fichero de respuestas sino el fundamento autoritativo sobre el cual se edifica todo recto razonamiento.

sa.prompt: 26. How do secular ethical systems locate the moral standard, and why does that finally fail?
sa.model: Strip away the labels and secular systems nearly all locate the standard somewhere inside the creation rather than in the Creator—in consequences, in reason, in the self, or, in our age, nowhere at all. The unit does not say these see nothing true; the man who weighs consequences is right that actions have results, and the relativist rightly notices that human judgments are fallible. The error is where they rest their weight: on the creature. A standard built on the creature can be no more stable, holy, or authoritative than the creature himself—preference dressed up as principle.

es_reference.prompt: 26. ¿Cómo ubican los sistemas éticos seculares la norma moral, y por qué fracasa eso finalmente?
es_reference.model: Quite las etiquetas y los sistemas seculares casi todos ubican la norma dentro de la creación en vez de en el Creador — en las consecuencias, en la razón, en el yo o, en nuestra época, en ninguna parte. La unidad no dice que no vean nada verdadero; el que pesa las consecuencias acierta en que las acciones tienen resultados, y el relativista nota que los juicios humanos son falibles. El error es dónde descansan su peso: sobre la criatura. Una norma edificada sobre la criatura no puede ser más estable, santa ni autoritativa que la criatura misma — preferencia disfrazada de principio.

sa.prompt: 27. Why does the unit say relativism cannot be lived? Use Romans 2:15.
sa.model: Relativism cannot be lived because the man who says there is no objective right and wrong will, the moment you wrong him, appeal to a justice he claims does not exist. He cannot help it, for he is made in the image of God and the work of the law is written on his heart (Romans 2:15). This is the pastor’s great point of contact: he is not importing a foreign morality but calling people back to the One whose law they already know in conscience and have spent their lives suppressing. The law the relativist cannot escape is the schoolmaster meant to bring him to Christ.

es_reference.prompt: 27. ¿Por qué dice la unidad que el relativismo no se puede vivir? Use Romanos 2:15.
es_reference.model: El relativismo no se puede vivir porque el hombre que dice que no hay bien ni mal objetivo, en el momento en que usted lo agravie, apelará a una justicia que afirma que no existe. No lo puede evitar, pues está hecho a imagen de Dios y la obra de la ley está escrita en su corazón (Romanos 2:15). Este es el gran punto de contacto del pastor: no importa una moral ajena sino que llama a las personas de vuelta a Aquel cuya ley ya conocen en la conciencia y han pasado la vida suprimiendo. La ley que el relativista no puede escapar es el ayo destinado a llevarlo a Cristo.

sa.prompt: 28. Why is a pastor held to a stricter standard, and what does James 3:1 teach about it?
sa.model: James 3:1 warns that not many should become teachers, knowing that teachers will receive a stricter judgment. The man who teaches others how to live has taken up a burden the ordinary believer has not, and God will not grade him on a curve because the work was hard. The teacher is judged as a teacher. That higher account should sober a pastor every time he opens the Book to instruct another soul.

es_reference.prompt: 28. ¿Por qué es tenido el pastor a una norma más estricta, y qué enseña Santiago 3:1 sobre ello?
es_reference.model: Santiago 3:1 advierte que no muchos se hagan maestros, sabiendo que los maestros recibirán mayor condenación. El hombre que enseña a otros cómo vivir ha tomado una carga que el creyente ordinario no ha tomado, y Dios no lo calificará con indulgencia porque la obra fuera difícil. Al maestro se le juzga como maestro. Esa cuenta más alta debería sobrecoger al pastor cada vez que abre el Libro para instruir a otra alma.

sa.prompt: 29. Explain the claim that pastoral character is “not something you do, it is something you are.”
sa.model: Peter charges elders to be examples to the flock, and Paul can say, “Imitate me, just as I also imitate Christ.” The heaviest part of pastoral ethics is that a man leads by what he is, not merely by what he says. You can preach a sermon you have not lived, but you cannot pastor a people you are not. A congregation absorbs a shepherd’s character more deeply than his words, and where the two contradict, the character wins the argument every time.

es_reference.prompt: 29. Explique la afirmación de que el carácter pastoral «no es algo que usted hace, es algo que usted es».
es_reference.model: Pedro encarga a los ancianos ser ejemplos de la grey, y Pablo puede decir: «Sed imitadores de mí, así como yo de Cristo». La parte más pesada de la ética pastoral es que el hombre dirige por lo que es, no meramente por lo que dice. Usted puede predicar un sermón que no ha vivido, pero no puede pastorear a un pueblo que no es. La congregación absorbe el carácter del pastor más profundamente que sus palabras, y donde los dos se contradigan, el carácter gana la discusión cada vez.

sa.prompt: 30. State the governing order of grace and works from Ephesians 2:10, and explain why the order matters.
sa.model: Ephesians 2:10 says we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them. We are not saved by good works but most certainly saved for them. The governing order is grace first, always first, and then the holy life grace produces. Keep that order and ethics becomes the joyful study of how a forgiven man learns to walk worthy of the One who bought him; reverse it, and ethics curdles into a law that crushes.

es_reference.prompt: 30. Exponga el orden rector de la gracia y las obras a partir de Efesios 2:10, y explique por qué importa el orden.
es_reference.model: Efesios 2:10 dice que somos hechura suya, creados en Cristo Jesús para buenas obras que Dios preparó de antemano para que anduviésemos en ellas. No somos salvos por las buenas obras, pero ciertamente somos salvos para ellas. El orden rector es la gracia primero, siempre primero, y luego la vida santa que la gracia produce. Mantenga ese orden y la ética se vuelve el estudio gozoso de cómo un hombre perdonado aprende a andar digno de Aquel que lo compró; inviértalo, y la ética se cuaja en una ley que aplasta.
